newsitem.title: USA: US production dip seen strike-related, short-lived.
newsitem.headline: US production dip seen strike-related, short-lived.

text.p: Despite some surprising soft spots, a disappointing report on U.S. manufacturing in October probably overstates industrial sector weakness, economists said on Friday.
Auto strikes that hampered production at General Motors plants last month took more steam out of the overall manufacturing economy than analysts expected.
As a result, U.S. industrial production fell 0.5 percent in October, underperforming a Reuters poll consensus forecast for a flat reading.

"We factored in the GM strike, but I guess it put more of a dent in the overall numbers than people expected. Even absent the auto strike, we were still down a bit," said Gary Schlossberg, senior economist at Wells Fargo Bank.
Excluding autos and auto parts, production fell 0.1 percent in October, according to the report released by the Federal Reserve Board Friday morning.
But modest strength in consumer spending should give producers a reason to boost output in coming months, analysts said.
A report on Thursday showed U.S. retail sales excluding autos rose 0.4 percent in October, and that growth should continue, said Paul Kasriel, money market economist at Northern Trust Co.

"Overall, you may get somewhat slower manufacturing in the fourth quarter, but if we get a pickup in final demand, that sets up stronger manufacturing activity in the first quarter of 1997," Kasriel said.
Weakness in the National Association of Purchasing Management's industrial index suggests continuing pressure on production, analysts said.
The NAPM index fell to 50.2, or barely expansionary, in October and has averaged 49.2 through 1996 so far.
"The fourth quarter could see a slowdown in production. It looks like it is going to go negative if it doesn't snap back soon," said Chris Rupkey, financial economist at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi,
Some analysts played down the magnitude of the October production decline, but, to others, it suggested greater weakness than originally expected.
"It calls into question the strength of the economy. I wouldn't use special factors to explain it away," Rupkey said.
"This is another figure that pushes off talk of (Federal Reserve monetary) tightening as far as the eye can see," Rupkey added.
The Fed's Federal Open Market Committee took no action on rates at its meeting Wednesday.
Yet expectations for a strong Christmas selling season bolstered analysts' hopes for a rebound in production in the next few months.
"Look to the leading edge sectors of the economy, like consumer spending and housing. We're starting to see signs of stirring there, and that should get production out of the hole," Scholssberg said.
